content: Iron deficiency anemia occurs when the body lacks enough iron to produce hemoglobin. Normal hemoglobin range is 12-16 g/dL for women and 14-18 g/dL for men. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, dizziness, and cold hands/feet. Treatment includes iron supplements (ferrous sulfate 325mg daily), iron-rich foods (red meat, spinach, lentils), and vitamin C to enhance absorption. Severe cases (Hb below 7 g/dL) may require IV iron or blood transfusion. Follow-up CBC recommended after 4-6 weeks of treatment.

Hypothyroidism is an underactive thyroid gland. Normal TSH range is 0.4-4.0 mIU/L; elevated TSH with low Free T4 confirms diagnosis. Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune) is the most common cause, confirmed by elevated Anti-TPO antibodies. Symptoms include fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, and depression. Treatment is levothyroxine (starting dose 25-50 mcg/day), taken on empty stomach 30 minutes before breakfast. TSH should be rechecked every 6-8 weeks until stable. Untreated hypothyroidism can lead to myxedema coma in severe cases.

Vitamin D deficiency is defined as serum 25(OH)D below 20 ng/mL; insufficiency is 20-29 ng/mL; optimal is 30-100 ng/mL. Symptoms include bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue, and mood changes. Risk factors include limited sun exposure, dark skin, obesity, and malabsorption disorders. Treatment: 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks (repletion), then 1000-2000 IU daily (maintenance). Dietary sources include fatty fish, fortified milk, egg yolks. Severe deficiency can cause osteomalacia in adults and rickets in children.

Type 2 diabetes diagnostic criteria: fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL. Prediabetes: fasting glucose 100-125, HbA1c 5.7-6.4%. First-line treatment is metformin plus lifestyle modification (150 min/week exercise, Mediterranean diet). Target HbA1c is generally below 7%. Monitor for complications: retinopathy (annual eye exam), nephropathy (annual urine albumin), neuropathy (foot exam). Hypoglycemia symptoms: shakiness, sweating, confusion — treat with 15g fast carbs.
source: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes, 2024

content: Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mmHg. Stage 1 hypertension: 130-139/80-89 mmHg. Stage 2: ≥140/90 mmHg. Hypertensive crisis: >180/120 mmHg (seek emergency care). First-line medications include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics. Lifestyle modifications: DASH diet, reduce sodium to <2300mg/day, regular exercise 150 min/week, limit alcohol, maintain healthy weight. Untreated hypertension increases risk of stroke, heart attack, kidney disease, and heart failure.

topic: Common Cold vs Flu vs COVID-19
content: Common cold: gradual onset, runny nose, sneezing, mild cough, rarely fever. Treatment is supportive (rest, fluids, OTC decongestants). Influenza (flu): sudden onset, high fever (100-104°F), severe body aches, extreme fatigue, dry cough. Antivirals (oseltamivir) effective within 48 hours. COVID-19: fever, dry cough, loss of taste/smell, fatigue, difficulty breathing. Key differentiator is loss of taste/smell (highly specific for COVID). All three are viral; antibiotics are NOT effective. Seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, or confusion.

Chest pain requires urgent evaluation. Cardiac causes: crushing/squeezing pain, radiating to left arm/jaw, associated with sweating, nausea, shortness of breath — CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY. Non-cardiac causes include GERD (burning, worse after eating), musculoskeletal (reproducible with palpation), anxiety (tingling, hyperventilation), pulmonary embolism (sudden onset with tachycardia). Diagnostic workup: ECG within 10 minutes, troponin levels, chest X-ray. Risk factors for cardiac: age >45 male/>55 female, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, family history. Never ignore new-onset chest pain.

Use FAST criteria: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency. Additional signs: sudden severe headache, vision loss, confusion, difficulty walking. Ischemic stroke (87% of cases) — tPA must be given within 4.5 hours. Hemorrhagic stroke — surgical intervention may be needed. Risk factors: hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, high cholesterol. Post-stroke care includes antiplatelet therapy, statin therapy, blood pressure management, and rehabilitation. Every minute of delay costs ~1.9 million neurons.

Pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma. Symptoms: productive cough, fever, chills, difficulty breathing, chest pain (pleuritic). Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) most common pathogen is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Diagnosis via chest X-ray showing consolidation, elevated WBC, procalcitonin. Treatment: amoxicillin for mild; azithromycin + beta-lactam for moderate. Hospitalization criteria (CURB-65): confusion, urea >7, respiratory rate >30, BP systolic <90, age ≥65. Complications include pleural effusion, empyema, sepsis. Vaccination (Pneumovax, Prevnar) recommended for elderly and immunocompromised.

Migraine is a primary headache disorder. Characteristics: unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe intensity, lasting 4-72 hours. Associated symptoms: nausea, vomiting, photophobia (light sensitivity), phonophobia (sound sensitivity). Aura occurs in 25% of cases (visual disturbances). Acute treatment: triptans (sumatriptan), NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400-800mg), antiemetics. Preventive therapy (for ≥4 attacks/month): propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, CGRP inhibitors. Triggers include stress, sleep changes, alcohol, MSG, hormonal changes, dehydration. Keep a headache diary for pattern identification.

UTI symptoms include burning urination (dysuria), frequency, urgency, cloudy/foul-smelling urine, suprapubic pain. E. coli causes 80% of cases. Diagnosis via urinalysis (positive leukocyte esterase, nitrites) and urine culture. Uncomplicated UTI treatment: nitrofurantoin 100mg BID x5 days or TMP-SMX x3 days. Complicated UTI (fever, flank pain) suggests pyelonephritis — needs fluoroquinolone or IV antibiotics. Prevention: adequate hydration, urinate after intercourse, cranberry products (limited evidence). Recurrent UTIs (≥3/year) may need prophylactic antibiotics.

Major depressive disorder: persistent low mood or anhedonia for ≥2 weeks, plus 4+ of: sleep changes, appetite/weight changes, fatigue, guilt/worthlessness, concentration difficulty, psychomotor changes, suicidal ideation. PHQ-9 score ≥10 suggests moderate depression. First-line treatment: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram) + psychotherapy (CBT). Response takes 4-6 weeks. Continue medication for ≥6-12 months after remission. Emergency: suicidal ideation with plan → immediate psychiatric evaluation. Helplines: National Suicide Prevention Lifeline 988, Crisis Text Line text HOME to 741741.
source: APA Clinical Practice Guidelines for Depression, 2023

content: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): excessive worry about multiple topics for ≥6 months, with 3+ of: restlessness, fatigue, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance. GAD-7 score ≥10 indicates moderate anxiety. Treatment: CBT (first-line), SSRIs/SNRIs, buspirone. Acute anxiety/panic: benzodiazepines short-term only (risk of dependence). Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected panic attacks with fear of future attacks. Lifestyle: regular exercise, sleep hygiene, limit caffeine/alcohol, mindfulness meditation.
source: APA Practice Guidelines for Anxiety Disorders, 2023

content: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable airflow obstruction. Symptoms: wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, cough (worse at night). Diagnosis: spirometry showing FEV1/FVC <0.70 with ≥12% reversibility after bronchodilator. Treatment stepwise: Step 1 — SABA as needed. Step 2 — low-dose ICS. Step 3 — low-dose ICS + LABA. Step 4 — medium-dose ICS + LABA. Asthma action plan is essential. Triggers: allergens, exercise, cold air, smoke, infections. Emergency: peak flow <50% predicted, cannot speak in sentences, cyanosis — call 911.
source: GINA Global Strategy for Asthma Management, 2024

content: GERD: chronic acid reflux causing heartburn (burning retrosternal pain), regurgitation, dysphagia. Diagnosis is clinical; upper endoscopy if alarm signs (weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding). Lifestyle modifications: elevate head of bed, avoid eating 3 hours before bed, lose weight, avoid trigger foods (spicy, acidic, caffeine, alcohol). Medications: PPIs (omeprazole 20mg before breakfast) for 8 weeks, then step down. Long-term PPI risks: vitamin B12 deficiency, magnesium deficiency, hip fractures. H. pylori testing recommended. Surgery (fundoplication) for refractory cases.

Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) present with severe unilateral flank pain (renal colic) radiating to groin, hematuria, nausea/vomiting. Types: calcium oxalate (80%), uric acid (10%), struvite (5%), cystine (1%). Diagnosis: CT KUB (non-contrast). Stones <5mm: 90% pass spontaneously with fluids and NSAIDs + tamsulosin (MET). Stones 5-10mm: 50% pass spontaneously. Stones >10mm: usually need lithotripsy (ESWL) or ureteroscopy. Prevention: drink 2.5L water daily, limit sodium, moderate calcium intake, reduce oxalate-rich foods.

Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. Symptoms: cyclic high fever with chills and rigors, sweating, headache, body aches, fatigue. P. falciparum causes severe malaria with cerebral involvement. Diagnosis: thick and thin blood smear, rapid diagnostic test (RDT). Treatment: uncomplicated — artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). Severe malaria — IV artesunate. Complications: cerebral malaria, severe anemia, renal failure, ARDS. Prevention: insecticide-treated nets, indoor spraying, chemoprophylaxis for travelers (atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine).

Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Symptoms: persistent cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis (coughing blood), night sweats, weight loss, fever. Diagnosis: chest X-ray, sputum AFB smear and culture, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, tuberculin skin test (PPD). Treatment: RIPE regimen — Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol for 2 months, then Isoniazid + Rifampin for 4 months. Add pyridoxine (B6) with isoniazid. Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) recommended. Drug-resistant TB requires modified regimens. Contacts should be screened.

Normal body temperature ranges 97.7-99.5°F (36.5-37.5°C). Fever defined as ≥100.4°F (38°C). Low-grade: 100.4-102.2°F; high: 102.2-104°F; hyperpyrexia: >104°F. Common causes: infections (viral most common), inflammatory conditions, malignancy. Red flags requiring emergency care: temperature >104°F, stiff neck/headache (meningitis), rash (meningococcemia), confusion, seizures, immunocompromised patient. Home management for mild fever: acetaminophen 500-1000mg or ibuprofen 400mg every 6-8 hours, adequate hydration, rest. Fever >3 days without obvious cause warrants medical evaluation.
source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition

content: Major modifiable risk factors: hypertension, hyperlipidemia (LDL >130), diabetes, smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyle. Non-modifiable: age (>45M, >55F), male sex, family history of premature CAD. Target LDL: <70 mg/dL for high risk, <100 for moderate risk. Statins are first-line for hyperlipidemia. Aspirin for secondary prevention (not routinely for primary). Lifestyle: Mediterranean diet, 150 min/week moderate exercise, smoking cessation, BMI <25, waist <40 inches (men) / <35 inches (women). Framingham Risk Score or ASCVD calculator for 10-year risk estimation.

Mild allergic reaction: localized hives, itching, mild swelling — treat with antihistamines (cetirizine, diphenhydramine). Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening reaction: generalized hives, throat swelling, difficulty breathing, hypotension, GI symptoms. TREATMENT: epinephrine IM (0.3-0.5mg of 1:1000) in lateral thigh — FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANT STEP. Call 911. Position: supine with legs elevated. Can repeat epinephrine every 5-15 minutes. Adjunct: H1/H2 blockers, corticosteroids, albuterol for bronchospasm. Observe 4-6 hours for biphasic reaction. All patients should carry EpiPen after first anaphylaxis.

COVID-19 caused by SARS-CoV-2. Current symptoms: fever, cough, fatigue, body aches, sore throat, congestion. Loss of taste/smell less common with newer variants. Testing: rapid antigen (less sensitive) or PCR. Mild cases: supportive care, hydration, rest, acetaminophen. High-risk patients: Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) within 5 days of symptoms. Isolation: 5 days if symptoms improving and fever-free 24 hours. Long COVID: fatigue, brain fog, dyspnea persisting >4 weeks. Emergency: difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, inability to stay awake.

Key liver markers: ALT (SGPT, normal 7-56 U/L), AST (SGOT, normal 10-40 U/L), ALP (44-147 U/L), bilirubin (0.1-1.2 mg/dL), albumin (3.5-5.0 g/dL). Elevated ALT/AST: hepatocellular damage (hepatitis, fatty liver, drug toxicity). ALT >AST suggests non-alcoholic cause; AST >ALT (2:1) suggests alcoholic liver disease. Elevated ALP + bilirubin: cholestatic pattern (bile duct obstruction, cholangitis). Low albumin: chronic liver disease, malnutrition. Elevated bilirubin: jaundice visible at >2.5 mg/dL. Further workup: hepatitis panel, ultrasound, fibroscan.
source: ACG Clinical Guidelines for Liver Disease, 2023

content: Normal CBC values: WBC 4,500-11,000/μL, RBC 4.5-5.5M/μL (men) 4.0-5.0M (women), Hemoglobin 14-18 g/dL (men) 12-16 g/dL (women), Hematocrit 40-54% (men) 36-48% (women), Platelets 150,000-400,000/μL, MCV 80-100 fL. Low WBC (leukopenia): viral infection, bone marrow suppression, autoimmune. High WBC (leukocytosis): bacterial infection, inflammation, leukemia. Low Hb: anemia (iron deficiency if MCV low, B12/folate if MCV high). Low platelets: ITP, DIC, liver disease. High platelets: reactive (infection, inflammation) or myeloproliferative disorder.

Acute low back pain: most cases are mechanical (muscle strain, ligament sprain) — resolves in 4-6 weeks. Red flags requiring urgent evaluation: age >50 or <20, fever, unexplained weight loss, bowel/bladder dysfunction (cauda equina syndrome — surgical emergency), progressive neurological deficit, history of cancer, IV drug use, trauma. Lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica): pain radiating below knee, positive straight leg raise. Treatment: stay active (bed rest worsens outcomes), NSAIDs, acetaminophen, muscle relaxants short-term. Physical therapy for chronic (>12 weeks). MRI only if red flags or failure to improve in 6 weeks.

TSH (0.4-4.0 mIU/L) is the primary screening test. High TSH + low Free T4 = primary hypothyroidism. Low TSH + high Free T4 = hyperthyroidism. High TSH + normal Free T4 = subclinical hypothyroidism. Anti-TPO antibodies: positive in Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune hypothyroidism). Anti-TSH receptor antibodies: positive in Graves' disease. Free T3 elevated disproportionately in early hyperthyroidism. Thyroglobulin: tumor marker for thyroid cancer follow-up. Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4-10): treat if symptomatic, pregnant, or Anti-TPO positive.

Mild dehydration (1-3% body weight loss): thirst, dry mouth, dark yellow urine, mild fatigue. Moderate (3-6%): decreased skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, reduced urine output. Severe (>6%): hypotension, shock, altered consciousness, no urine output. Causes: vomiting, diarrhea, excessive sweating, inadequate intake, diabetes (polyuria). Treatment: mild — oral rehydration (ORS or water with electrolytes). Moderate-severe — IV normal saline or Ringer's lactate. Monitor urine output (target >0.5 mL/kg/hr). Special populations: elderly and children dehydrate faster.

Common rash patterns: Maculopapular (viral exanthem, drug reaction, measles). Vesicular/bullous (herpes, varicella, contact dermatitis). Urticarial (allergic reaction, hives). Petechial/purpura (meningococcemia — emergency, thrombocytopenia, vasculitis). Scaling (psoriasis, eczema, fungal infection). Key questions: onset timing, distribution, associated symptoms (fever, itching), medication changes, exposures. Red flags: petechiae + fever (meningococcemia), widespread blistering (Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN), expanding bull's-eye (Lyme disease). Photos help remote assessment.
source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine, 9th Edition

content: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): blood glucose >250, ketones positive, pH <7.30, bicarbonate <18. Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing, altered consciousness. Treatment: IV insulin drip, aggressive IV fluids (NS), potassium replacement, monitor every 1-2 hours. Hypoglycemia: glucose <70 mg/dL. Symptoms: tremor, sweating, palpitations, confusion, seizures. Treatment: conscious — 15g fast carbs (glucose tablets, juice), recheck in 15 min. Unconscious — glucagon 1mg IM or IV dextrose. Both are medical emergencies requiring immediate intervention.

PTSD develops after exposure to traumatic event. Diagnostic criteria (DSM-5): intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative mood/cognition changes, arousal/reactivity changes (hypervigilance, insomnia, irritability), duration >1 month, significant distress. First-line treatment: trauma-focused CBT, prolonged exposure therapy, EMDR. Medications: sertraline or paroxetine (FDA-approved for PTSD). Prazosin for PTSD-related nightmares. Avoid benzodiazepines (worsen outcomes). Crisis resources: Veterans Crisis Line 988 (press 1), Crisis Text Line text HOME to 741741.

Acute gastroenteritis: vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, fever. Viral (norovirus, rotavirus) most common — self-limiting 1-3 days. Bacterial (Salmonella, E. coli, Campylobacter): bloody diarrhea, higher fever, longer duration. Treatment: oral rehydration is primary treatment. BRAT diet (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) during recovery. Antidiarrheals (loperamide) for non-bloody diarrhea only. Seek medical care if: bloody stool, fever >102°F, dehydration signs, symptoms >3 days, immunocompromised. Stool culture if bloody diarrhea or prolonged illness.

Normal B12: 200-900 pg/mL. Deficiency <200 pg/mL. Causes: pernicious anemia (intrinsic factor deficiency), vegetarian/vegan diet, metformin use, malabsorption (celiac, Crohn's). Symptoms: macrocytic anemia (high MCV), fatigue, glossitis, paresthesias (tingling in hands/feet), cognitive changes, balance problems. Neurological damage can be irreversible if untreated >6 months. Treatment: IM cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily x7 days, then weekly x4 weeks, then monthly. Oral B12 2000 mcg daily for dietary deficiency. Monitor with CBC and reticulocyte count.
source: British Society for Haematology B12 Guidelines, 2023

content: Osteoarthritis (OA): degenerative, affects weight-bearing joints, worse with activity, better with rest, bone spurs on X-ray. Treatment: exercise, weight loss, acetaminophen/NSAIDs, topical diclofenac, joint replacement if severe. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): autoimmune, symmetric small joint involvement, morning stiffness >1 hour, elevated RF and anti-CCP. Treatment: DMARDs (methotrexate first-line), biologics (TNF inhibitors). Gout: acute monoarthritis (big toe), uric acid >7 mg/dL, needle-shaped crystals on joint aspiration. Acute: colchicine/NSAIDs/steroids. Chronic: allopurinol/febuxostat.

First seizure evaluation: CT/MRI brain, EEG, basic labs (glucose, electrolytes, toxicology). Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24h apart. Generalized tonic-clonic: loss of consciousness, stiffening, jerking. Absence: brief staring spells. Focal: one body region, may preserve consciousness. FIRST AID: protect from injury, turn on side, do NOT put anything in mouth, time the seizure. Call 911 if: first seizure, lasts >5 minutes, no recovery after, injury, in water, pregnant. Medications: levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate (avoid in pregnancy). Status epilepticus (>5 min): IV benzodiazepines urgently.

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT): unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, redness. Risk factors: immobility, surgery, cancer, oral contraceptives, long flights. Diagnosis: D-dimer (if negative, rules out DVT), compression ultrasound. Pulmonary embolism (PE): sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis. Massive PE: hypotension, shock. Diagnosis: CT pulmonary angiography. Treatment: anticoagulation — heparin bridge to warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: rivaroxaban, apixaban). Duration: 3-6 months, longer if unprovoked. IVC filter if anticoagulation contraindicated.

Bipolar I: manic episodes (elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased sleep, pressured speech, risky behavior) lasting ≥1 week. Bipolar II: hypomanic + depressive episodes. Mania requires hospitalization if severe (psychosis, danger to self/others). First-line mood stabilizers: lithium (monitor levels, thyroid, renal), valproate, lamotrigine (depressive episodes). Atypical antipsychotics: quetiapine, olanzapine. Antidepressants alone can trigger mania — always pair with mood stabilizer. Maintenance treatment is lifelong. Psychoeducation and regular sleep schedule are essential.

Pneumothorax: air in pleural space causing lung collapse. Spontaneous: tall thin males, smoking. Traumatic: chest injury. Tension pneumothorax: life-threatening — tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, hypotension. IMMEDIATE treatment: needle decompression (2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line) then chest tube. Simple pneumothorax <20%: observation, supplemental oxygen. >20% or symptomatic: chest tube drainage. Symptoms: sudden sharp chest pain, shortness of breath, tachycardia. Chest X-ray shows visible pleural line. Recurrence rate 30% — consider pleurodesis for recurrent cases.

Vertigo (room spinning) vs lightheadedness vs presyncope vs disequilibrium. BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo): brief episodes triggered by head position changes, positive Dix-Hallpike test. Treatment: Epley maneuver (90% effective). Vestibular neuritis: acute severe vertigo lasting days, no hearing loss. Treatment: vestibular rehabilitation, short-term meclizine. Meniere's disease: episodic vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + ear fullness. Central vertigo red flags: vertical nystagmus, skew deviation, acute severe headache, focal neurological deficits — MRI urgently to rule out stroke.

Sickle cell disease: inherited hemoglobinopathy (HbSS). Vaso-occlusive crisis: severe pain (bones, chest, abdomen) due to sickling. Treatment: IV fluids, opioids for pain, oxygen if hypoxic. Acute chest syndrome: new pulmonary infiltrate + fever/chest pain — treat with antibiotics, exchange transfusion. Stroke risk: transcranial Doppler screening annually. Disease-modifying: hydroxyurea (increases HbF), L-glutamine, voxelotor, crizanlizumab. Chronic complications: avascular necrosis, renal disease, pulmonary hypertension. Genetic counseling for carriers.

Drug allergy vs side effect vs intolerance. IgE-mediated (immediate, within 1 hour): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis. Common culprits: penicillins, NSAIDs, sulfonamides. T-cell mediated (delayed, days-weeks): maculopapular rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, DRESS syndrome. SJS/TEN: mucocutaneous blistering >30% BSA — dermatology emergency (30% mortality). Key: document exact reaction, cross-reactivity patterns (penicillin-cephalosporin <2%), desensitization protocols available for essential drugs. Never rechallenge with a drug that caused anaphylaxis or SJS/TEN.

Location-based differential: RUQ — gallstones, hepatitis, cholecystitis. Epigastric — GERD, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis. LUQ — splenic pathology, gastric ulcer. RLQ — appendicitis (McBurney's point tenderness, rebound), ovarian pathology. LLQ — diverticulitis, sigmoid pathology. Diffuse — gastroenteritis, mesenteric ischemia, bowel obstruction, peritonitis. Red flags: rigid abdomen (peritonitis), fever + localized pain, vomiting blood, black tarry stools, severe sudden onset (perforation/rupture). Labs: CBC, CMP, lipase, UA, pregnancy test. Imaging: CT abdomen with contrast.
source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria for Abdominal Pain, 2023

content: Insomnia: difficulty falling/staying asleep ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months. First-line treatment: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I), not medications. Sleep hygiene: consistent schedule, dark/cool room, no screens 1hr before bed, no caffeine after noon, limit alcohol. Medications (short-term): zolpidem, suvorexant, trazodone. Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness. Diagnosis: polysomnography (AHI ≥5). Treatment: CPAP, weight loss, positional therapy. Untreated OSA increases risk of hypertension, stroke, MI, accidents.

Normal pregnancy symptoms: nausea, fatigue, breast tenderness, frequent urination. Warning signs requiring IMMEDIATE medical attention: vaginal bleeding (miscarriage, placenta previa), severe headache + vision changes + swelling (preeclampsia), sudden severe abdominal pain (ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption), decreased fetal movement (<10 kicks in 2 hours), gush of fluid (premature rupture of membranes), fever >100.4°F, burning urination (UTI can cause preterm labor). Preeclampsia criteria: BP >140/90 + proteinuria after 20 weeks — can progress to eclampsia (seizures). HELLP syndrome: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets.

Anorexia nervosa: BMI <18.5 with fear of weight gain, body image distortion, food restriction. Medical complications: bradycardia, amenorrhea, osteoporosis, electrolyte imbalances (fatal arrhythmias with hypokalemia), refeeding syndrome. Bulimia nervosa: binge eating + compensatory behaviors (purging, laxatives, excessive exercise). Complications: dental erosion, Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), metabolic alkalosis. Binge eating disorder: recurrent binges without compensatory behaviors. Treatment for all: multidisciplinary — psychiatrist, psychologist (CBT, FBT for adolescents), nutritionist. Hospitalize if medically unstable.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder: recurrent intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors/mental acts (compulsions) that are time-consuming (≥1 hour/day) and cause significant distress. Common types: contamination/washing, symmetry/ordering, harm/checking, forbidden thoughts. First-line treatment: CBT with Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) — gold standard. Medications: high-dose SSRIs (fluoxetine 40-80mg, fluvoxamine). Augmentation: low-dose antipsychotic (aripiprazole) if partial response. Treatment duration: minimum 1-2 years. Y-BOCS scale for severity monitoring. Not same as OCPD (personality trait).

topic: When to Go to the Emergency Room
content: Go to ER immediately for: chest pain or pressure, signs of stroke (FAST), difficulty breathing, severe allergic reaction, uncontrolled bleeding, loss of consciousness, seizure (first-time), severe abdominal pain, high fever with stiff neck (meningitis), suicidal thoughts with plan, severe head injury, poisoning/overdose, severe burns, compound fractures. Go to urgent care (not ER) for: minor cuts/burns, sprains, UTI symptoms, mild allergic reactions, ear/sinus infections, mild asthma exacerbation. Call primary doctor for: chronic condition management, medication refills, non-urgent lab results, preventive care.

ADHD: persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning. Presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, combined. Diagnosis requires symptoms in ≥2 settings, onset before age 12, lasting ≥6 months. Assessment tools: Conners Rating Scales, ASRS (Adult ADHD Self-Report). First-line treatment: stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine salts) — 70-80% response rate. Non-stimulant alternatives: atomoxetine, guanfacine. Behavioral therapy especially important for children. Adults benefit from organizational coaching, CBT. Monitor growth, BP, heart rate on stimulants.

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) staging by GFR: Stage 1 (≥90, with markers), Stage 2 (60-89), Stage 3a (45-59), Stage 3b (30-44), Stage 4 (15-29), Stage 5 (<15, dialysis). Key markers: elevated creatinine, decreased GFR, proteinuria (UACR >30 mg/g). Most common causes: diabetes and hypertension. Complications: anemia (erythropoietin deficiency), hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, mineral bone disease, fluid overload. Management: BP control (<130/80), ACEi/ARB for proteinuria, glycemic control, low-sodium diet, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast dye). Refer to nephrology at Stage 4.

Normal lipid values: total cholesterol <200, LDL <100 (optimal), HDL >40 (men) >50 (women), triglycerides <150. LDL targets: very high risk <55 (statin + ezetimibe), high risk <70, moderate risk <100. First-line: high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40-80mg or rosuvastatin 20-40mg). If statin-intolerant: ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, PCSK9 inhibitors. Lifestyle: Mediterranean diet, increase fiber, reduce saturated fat, exercise 150 min/week, weight loss. Triglycerides >500: risk of pancreatitis — add fibrate or omega-3 (4g/day). Recheck lipids in 6-12 weeks after starting therapy.

Burn depth: first-degree (epidermis only, red, painful — like sunburn), second-degree (blistering, very painful), third-degree (full thickness, white/charred, painless). Rule of Nines for BSA estimation. Minor burns (<10% BSA, second-degree): cool running water 20 minutes (NOT ice), aloe vera, non-stick dressing, acetaminophen/ibuprofen. Seek ER for: burns >10% BSA, third-degree, face/hands/feet/genitals, circumferential, chemical, electrical, inhalation. Fluid resuscitation for major burns: Parkland formula (4mL × kg × %BSA/24h). Tetanus prophylaxis if not up to date.

Iron studies panel: serum iron (60-170 μg/dL), TIBC (250-370 μg/dL), transferrin saturation (20-50%), ferritin (12-150 ng/mL women, 12-300 ng/mL men). Iron deficiency anemia: low ferritin (<12), low iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation. Anemia of chronic disease: low iron, low TIBC, normal/high ferritin. Iron overload (hemochromatosis): high ferritin (>300 men, >200 women), high transferrin saturation (>45%). Ferritin is also acute phase reactant — can be falsely elevated with inflammation. Consider soluble transferrin receptor if ferritin unreliable.
